h1: Olive Oil for Roasting Vegetables: How to Get Them to Actually Crisp
excerpt: Most roasted vegetables come out of the oven soft and grey instead of browned at the edges. The fix is rarely the oven. It is how much oil goes on, how the tray is loaded, and when the salt lands.
keyTakeaway: Coat vegetables in a thin film of oil, about a tablespoon per tray, not a pool. Spread them in one uncrowded layer so steam escapes, roast hot for watery vegetables and lower for dense ones, salt dense vegetables before and watery ones after, then finish with a raw drizzle once out.

inlineAlt: Green olive oil in a glass bottle
intro: A tray of roasted vegetables that comes out pale and soft instead of browned at the edges has usually not failed because of the oven. It has failed because of the oil and the tray: too little coating, too much crowding, or salt added at the wrong moment.
None of that needs more heat. It needs less vegetable per tray and a clearer idea of what each one wants.

sections.heading: How much oil actually belongs on the tray

blocks.text: A tray of cut vegetables needs a thin, even coating of olive oil, not a puddle at the bottom. For a full baking sheet, start with about a tablespoon and toss until every piece looks glossy rather than wet, adding more only if dry patches remain.

Too little oil and the cut surfaces dry out and char before they soften. Too much and the vegetables sit in a shallow fry instead of a roast. See the [smoke point guide](/blog/olive-oil-smoke-point-what-heat-it-can-take) for how far extra virgin can be pushed.

sections.heading: Why a crowded tray is the real enemy of crisping

blocks.text: Vegetables piled two and three deep release water as they heat, and that water has nowhere to go in a crowded pan — it collects, and they steam in it instead of browning. One layer with visible gaps between pieces lets the moisture escape upward instead of pooling.
If the tray is covered edge to edge with no gaps, split the batch across two trays. A half-empty tray is usually the one that browns properly.

sections.heading: Oven temperature and roughly how long, by vegetable

blocks.text: Dense root vegetables want a lower oven and more time so the inside cooks through before the outside burns. Watery, quick-cooking vegetables want it hot and fast, so they brown before turning to mush. The table below is a starting point, not a fixed rule.
Cut pieces roughly the same size on one tray so they finish together, flipping halfway if one side browns faster.

sections.heading: When to salt: before the oven or after

blocks.text: Dense vegetables such as potatoes, carrots and pumpkin can take salt before they go in, since it has time to season through as they cook. Watery vegetables such as zucchini, eggplant and tomatoes are better salted after, since salt draws water out and an early hand slows the browning.

items: **Salt before.** Dense roots, cauliflower, broccoli, onions.
**Salt after.** Zucchini, eggplant, cherry tomatoes, mushrooms.
**Either works.** Bell peppers and asparagus, since they hold little water.

sections.heading: Which vegetables want hot and fast versus low and slow

blocks.text: The split is about water content and density, not the vegetable's family. Thin, watery pieces want a hot oven and a short time so they brown before they collapse; thick, dense pieces want a gentler oven so the centre catches up before the outside burns.

items: **Hot and fast.** Asparagus, cherry tomatoes, zucchini, thin green beans — in and out in under twenty minutes.
**Low and longer.** Whole beetroot, large potato wedges, pumpkin chunks, whole garlic bulbs — closer to forty-five to fifty minutes.

sections.heading: The raw drizzle after the tray comes out

blocks.text: A second, raw pour of extra virgin olive oil after roasting is a different job from the oil the vegetables cooked in. The heated oil is a cooking medium; the finishing oil is tasted straight, so its own flavour — grassy, peppery, herbal — is what the diner notices first.

A teaspoon or two over the tray, added while the vegetables are still hot enough to carry the aroma, does more for the finished dish than any amount added before roasting. An infused oil such as [rosemary and basil](/products) suits this step well, since none of its aroma is lost to the oven.

A thin coating, not a pool. One uncrowded layer. Hot and fast for watery vegetables, lower and longer for dense ones. Salt dense vegetables before, watery ones after, and finish with a raw drizzle once the tray is out.

faqs.q: How much olive oil should I use for roasted vegetables?
faqs.a: About a tablespoon per full baking tray, tossed until every piece looks glossy rather than wet. Add a little more only if dry patches remain — a pool at the bottom is too much oil.

faqs.q: Why do my roasted vegetables come out soggy instead of crispy?
faqs.a: The tray is usually too crowded. Piled vegetables release water with nowhere to go, so they steam instead of browning. Spread them in one layer with visible gaps, splitting into two trays if needed.

faqs.q: What oven temperature is best for roasting vegetables?
faqs.a: It depends on the vegetable. Dense roots like potatoes and beetroot suit 200-220°C for 35-45 minutes; watery, quick-cooking vegetables like asparagus and cherry tomatoes want a hotter 220-230°C for closer to 10-20 minutes.

faqs.q: Should I salt vegetables before or after roasting?
faqs.a: Dense vegetables such as potatoes can be salted before, since it seasons through as they cook. Watery vegetables such as zucchini and tomatoes are better salted after, since early salt slows browning.

faqs.q: Should I use extra virgin olive oil for roasting?
faqs.a: Yes, extra virgin comfortably handles oven roasting inside the published 180-200°C range. See the [smoke point guide](/blog/olive-oil-smoke-point-what-heat-it-can-take) for the full range it can take before it starts to smoke.

faqs.q: Why add more olive oil after the vegetables are roasted?
faqs.a: A raw drizzle is tasted straight rather than cooked away, so its own flavour comes through. A teaspoon or two while the tray is still hot carries more aroma than oil added before cooking starts.

faqs.q: Can I roast all vegetables together on one tray?
faqs.a: Only if they cook at similar speeds. Mixing quick asparagus with whole beetroot means one burns before the other softens through — group vegetables by roughly how long each one needs instead.
